draft.title: Weathering and erosion
card: the breaking down of rock where it sits, with no movement of the pieces. It can be physical, such as water freezing in a crack and splitting the rock, or chemical, such as rainwater slowly dissolving limestone.
the wearing away of land and the carrying of the pieces to another place by water, wind or ice.
Weathering usually comes first. It loosens rock into smaller pieces, and these pieces are then easier for water, wind or ice to carry away.
Over time, erosion shapes landforms. Waves cut cliffs, rivers carve valleys, wind builds dunes and glaciers gouge out hollows.
draft.remember: Weathering breaks rock in place. Erosion moves the pieces away.

a.q: Which description is an example of weathering rather than erosion?
opts: Rock in a cliff cracks as water freezes in a gap
A river carries sand and gravel down to a lake
Wind lifts dry sand and drops it as a new dune
Waves pull loose rock from a cliff base out to sea
a.why: The rock cracks and stays where it is, so this is weathering. The other three all involve moving pieces of rock or sand to another place, which is erosion. The river option is tempting, but carrying sand and gravel away is erosion.
a.clue: Look for the rock breaking up without being moved.

b.q: On a dry hillside in western NSW, rock slowly splits into small stones during hot days and cold nights. After a storm, running water washes the stones into a creek bed. Which pair of terms fits these two steps in order?
opts: Weathering, then erosion
Erosion, then weathering
Weathering, then weathering
Erosion, then erosion
b.why: The rock splitting where it sits is weathering. The storm water then carries the stones away, which is erosion. Erosion cannot come first here, because the water only moves pieces that weathering has already loosened.
b.clue: Ask which step moves the pieces and which step only breaks them.

a.best: Rock in a cliff cracks as water freezes in a gap

problems.detail: The card says erosion shapes landforms and gives 'wind builds dunes' as an example. Dunes are built by deposition, where wind drops the sand it has carried, not by erosion. A better example would be wind scouring or sandblasting rock, or the card could say that erosion and deposition together shape landforms.
